subsection: 2. Economic planning and the move to free trade; case study: the First Programme for Economic Expansion, 1958–1963

notes.b: By 1957 the economy was stagnant, with rising emigration and a persistent balance of payments deficit.
points: Protectionism under the Control of Manufactures Acts of 1932 and 1934 had shielded Irish industry from foreign competition but kept most firms small and inefficient.
Irish exports were concentrated on agricultural goods sold to Britain, so the economy depended closely on British demand.
Under the Inter-Party governments, budgets had been deflationary and reactive, with no long-term investment programme.
Seán Lemass, as Minister for Industry and Commerce from 1957, pressed for a policy of expansion and an end to protectionist barriers.

notes.h: Economic Development (1958) and the First Programme
notes.b: T.K. Whitaker, Secretary of the Department of Finance, wrote the policy document that set the state's economic direction.
points: Economic Development, published in 1958, argued that growth in output and exports was needed to cut emigration and unemployment.
It proposed a planned approach, in which the state set targets and then coordinated public and private investment to meet them.
The First Programme for Economic Expansion was launched in October 1958 to run from 1959 to 1963.
Its central aim was to raise national output by a set percentage over the programme period, with a target of about 50 per cent growth in gross national product (about, verify).
Programme targets were published in advance, so that progress could be measured against them each year.
Grants and tax relief were offered to exporters and to firms that expanded production, to encourage new investment.
Foreign investment was invited on more generous terms, with the Control of Manufactures Acts relaxed so that overseas firms could set up plants in Ireland.
Public investment was directed at productive projects such as electricity, roads and industrial infrastructure, rather than at welfare or current spending.
Agricultural productivity was encouraged, with support for farm modernisation and export marketing.
The programme was prepared by the Department of Finance and drew on advisers in the civil service and the Central Bank.

notes.b: Results are judged against the programme's own targets, which were partly met and partly missed.
points: Industrial exports and manufacturing output grew substantially in the early 1960s, though the exact growth rate is disputed (verify before quoting).
Foreign direct investment grew, and firms such as those in electronics and chemicals established factories in the period.
Emigration fell from its 1950s peak, with the net outflow declining in the early 1960s.
Unemployment remained high, and the programme did not eliminate the balance of payments problem.
Some targets, such as employment creation, were not achieved, which later critics stressed.

notes.b: Lemass became Taoiseach in June 1959 when de Valera became President, and he pushed the programme forward and extended it.
points: Lemass's style was pragmatic and managerial, and he promoted the image of a modern, outward-looking state.
A Second Programme for Economic Expansion was launched in 1963 to continue the planning approach.
The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement was signed in December 1965, cutting tariffs on trade between Ireland and Britain.

Lemass met the Northern Ireland Prime Minister Terence O'Neill in Belfast in January 1965 and in Dublin in February 1965, the first such meetings since partition (see the notes on Anglo-Irish relations).
Lemass applied for membership of the European Economic Community on 31 July 1961, linking Irish trade policy to the common market (see the notes on the United Nations and the EEC).

notes.h: Case study: the aims, measures and results of the First Programme
points: Aim: to raise living standards by expanding output and exports, and to create jobs to reduce emigration.
Method: planning through published targets, with public investment and tax incentives to encourage private investment.
Outcome: economic growth in the early 1960s was faster than in the 1950s, with a notable rise in industrial output.
Limit: the state's economy remained dependent on Britain for its markets, so tariff reductions were a major step.
Significance: the programme marked the start of economic planning as a regular function of the Irish state.

notes.h: Free trade and the EEC application
points: The first EEC application in 1961 was blocked when Charles de Gaulle, President of France, vetoed British membership in January 1963; Ireland's application was tied to Britain's.
The move to free trade meant accepting lower tariffs on imports, which threatened protected Irish industries.
Critics feared the closure of small firms that could not compete with foreign products.
Supporters argued that free trade would bring cheaper inputs, export markets and new investment.

notes.b: Whitaker was the civil servant who drafted the planning document, not a politician, and his role was central to the programme.
points: Thomas Kenneth Whitaker was Secretary of the Department of Finance from 1956 and wrote Economic Development in 1958.
He had worked with Lemass in planning the programme and was regarded as the architect of its approach.
Contemporaries praised his clear analysis, though some politicians and officials were wary of planning for its loss of control over budgets.
Historians credit him with shifting Irish economic policy from reaction to planned growth, and he later served as Governor of the Central Bank (about 1969–1976, verify).
Seán Lemass was a Fianna Fáil minister from 1932 and Taoiseach from 1959 to 1966.
He had been Minister for Industry and Commerce from 1932 to 1939 and from 1957 to 1959, and he backed the move away from protectionism.
Contemporary views saw him as a modernising leader who promoted technology, tourism and industry.
Historians judge him more favourably on economic modernisation, but they note that his government left unemployment and rural poverty unresolved.

notes.h: Assessment: the First Programme and its significance
points: Achievements: the programme set a planning model that later governments followed, and it coincided with a rise in investment and exports.
Limits: targets for jobs and regional development were not fully met, and the balance of payments remained a constraint.
Contemporary view: it was widely welcomed as a break from the stagnation of the 1950s.
Later view: historians present it as a turning point, but they disagree over how far growth was caused by the programme rather than by external conditions.

keyTerms.definition: A policy of setting published economic targets and coordinating public and private investment to meet them over a set period.
A policy of removing or reducing tariffs and trade barriers so that goods and investment move more freely between countries.
The 1958 policy document by T.K. Whitaker that proposed a planned programme of growth for the Irish economy.
The 1932 and 1934 acts that protected Irish industry from foreign competition and restricted foreign ownership of manufacturing.
The December 1965 agreement between Ireland and Britain that began a phased reduction of tariffs on trade between the two countries.
The use of tariffs and import controls to shield domestic industry from foreign competition.

factCards.term: First Programme for Economic Expansion: dates
factCards.definition: The First Programme ran from 1959 to 1963 and was launched in October 1958.
T.K. Whitaker, Secretary of the Department of Finance, wrote Economic Development in 1958.
Seán Lemass became Taoiseach in June 1959 and held office until 1966.

factCards.term: Date of the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement
factCards.definition: The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement was signed in December 1965, cutting tariffs on trade between Ireland and Britain.
Lemass and Terence O'Neill met in Belfast in January 1965 and in Dublin in February 1965.

factCards.term: Date of the first EEC application
factCards.definition: Ireland applied to join the European Economic Community on 31 July 1961, alongside Britain.
In January 1963 President Charles de Gaulle of France vetoed British membership of the EEC, which halted the Irish application.
The Second Programme was launched in 1963 to continue the planning approach begun in 1958.
Whitaker became Governor of the Central Bank of Ireland around 1969 (about, verify end date).
Lemass was Minister for Industry and Commerce from 1932 to 1939 and again from 1957 to 1959.

factCards.term: Target for growth in the First Programme
factCards.definition: The First Programme aimed for about a 50 per cent increase in gross national product over its five years (about, verify).

factCards.term: Use of the Control of Manufactures Acts in the 1960s
factCards.definition: The Control of Manufactures Acts were relaxed in the early 1960s so that foreign firms could set up plants in Ireland.
